There is a particular kind of quiet that only exists in the early hours, before the first delivery truck rattles down the street and before the kettle has been filled for the day. I find myself drawn to it. In that quiet, ordinary things seem to wake up slowly, like a cat stretching on a windowsill. The refrigerator hums its one long note. A single bird tests a few tentative phrases from somewhere in the dark maple outside, as if checking whether the morning is really going to happen.

I've been thinking lately about maps, especially the old ones. Early cartographers filled the blank edges of their work with sea monsters, curling waves, and cherubic faces blowing wind across the oceans. Some of those drawings were guesses, some were decorations, and some were simply the mapmakers admitting that they did not know what lay beyond. I find that honesty appealing. Our own maps are sharper and more confident, yet we still have unexplored corners, both in the world and in ourselves.

Then there is the matter of handwriting. A letter written by hand carries small evidence of its author: a pressed-harder word here, a crossed-out sentence there, the slight slant that gives away a moment of hurry or care. Typed messages are efficient, but they rarely tell you how the writer felt while producing them.

Perhaps that is why I keep a notebook by the bed. Most entries are unremarkable, just lists and half-formed thoughts. But reading them later, I find traces of who I was on those particular mornings, listening to the same bird, waiting for the same light to arrive.
